title: Diwali, the Festival of Lights, Is Celebrated Today
summary:
Diwali is the most important festival of the year in India, particularly for Hindus, and it is widely marked by prayers, family gatherings, and the lighting of fireworks. More than one billion people across faiths celebrate it in the world's most populous nation and its diaspora. This year, Diwali falls on November 8.

The name Diwali comes from "Deepavali," meaning "a row of lights." Celebrants place rows of traditional clay oil lamps outside their homes to symbolize the victory of light over darkness and knowledge over ignorance. The festival follows the Hindu lunar calendar, typically falling in late October or early November.

While Diwali is a major religious festival for Hindus, it is also observed by Sikhs, Jains, and Buddhists. Its origin stories vary by region but share a theme: the victory of good over evil. In southern India, Diwali celebrates Lord Krishna's victory over the demon Naraka, who is said to have imprisoned women and tormented his subjects. In northern India, it honors the triumphant return of Lord Rama, his wife, Sita, and his brother, Lakshmana, after 14 years of exile in the forest.

Traditions vary by region but commonly include lights, fireworks, feasting, new clothes, and prayers. In southern India, many people take an early morning bath with warm oil to symbolize bathing in the holy River Ganges for physical and spiritual purification. In the north, worship centers on the goddess Lakshmi, who symbolizes wealth and prosperity. Gambling is a popular tradition, reflecting a belief that those who gamble on Diwali night will prosper throughout the year. Many people buy gold on Dhanteras, the first day of the festival, believing it will bring good luck.

Jains observe Diwali as the day Lord Mahavira, the last of their great teachers, attained nirvana, or liberation from the cycle of birth, death, and rebirth. Sikhs celebrate Bandi Chhor Divas, which overlaps with Diwali, to commemorate the release of Guru Hargobind from imprisonment under the Mughal emperor Jahangir. Some Buddhists mark the day as the anniversary of Emperor Ashoka's conversion to Buddhism in the third century B.C.

Diwali is also celebrated far beyond India. Disney World in Florida held several days of Diwali festivities ahead of the holiday, featuring more than 500 dancers. Diwali at Times Square marked its 11th year in New York City with international performers, cultural bazaars, and a lighting countdown at the Ball Drop Tower. Other community events across North America include Diwali Eve on the Waterfront in Jersey City, a Diwali Family Cruise on the Hudson in New York, Diwali on the Bay in San Francisco, and a Diwali Fusion Bollywood Boat Party in Vancouver, British Columbia.
why_it_matters: Diwali shows how one festival can carry different stories for different faiths while sharing the same hope that light wins over darkness. For the many families who celebrate it far from India, it is also a way to keep their culture alive in a new home.
